newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Japan's Hashimoto visits Uncle Ho's mausoleum.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Hashimoto visits Uncle Ho's mausoleum.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto wound up the fourth stage of a swing through Southeast Asia on Sunday, paying homage at the mausoleum of communist Vietnam's founding father, Ho Chi Minh, before he left Hanoi.

The Japanese leader was due to land in Singapore in the middle of the afternoon, where he will cap his five-nation tour on Tuesday with a key policy speech pledging closer ties with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
Billed by Tokyo as a landmark push to take its relations with the region beyond the economic sphere, Hashimoto's tour has been overshadowed by the 25-day-old hostage crisis in Lima.
The crisis entered a more hopeful phase on Saturday as the government and Marxist rebels who are holding 74 people in the Japanese ambassador's residence prepared to resume talks.
Hashimoto, apparently wearing a bullet-proof vest, laid flowers at Ho Chi Minh's mausoleum and then went inside the monolith to view the revolutionary leader's embalmed corpse.
"Uncle Ho" was the founder of the Viet Minh, which resisted the Japanese occupation of Vietnam during World War Two.
That era lives on in the memory of many older Vietnamese people. But the two countries' governments have consigned it to the history books and forged ever-stronger links.

On his arrival in Hanoi on Saturday, Hashimoto met Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet and then signed a stack of new aid pledges worth some $765 million -- mostly loans to improve the poverty-hit country's creaking infrastructure.
Tokyo is by far and away poverty-hit Vietnam's leading donor, pledging $3.23 billion between 1992 and 1996. Of the record $2.4 billion committed by donors for this year, its share is about one third.
Japan is also Vietnam's biggest trading partner and ranks second among foreign investors in the booming economy.
Japanese Foreign Ministry Spokesman Ken Shimanouchi told reporters on Saturday that Hashimoto had promised continued support for Hanoi's decade-old economic reform drive.

However, he said Hashimoto had stressed his desire to widen the scope of relations to embrace regional security, cultural, environmental and other areas -- a message he had already taken to Brunei, Malaysia and Indonesia and will repeat in Singapore.
All five countries are members of the seven-nation ASEAN grouping, which Vietnam joined in 1995.
Simanouchi shrugged off suggestions by reporters that Japan's drive for security cooperation with ASEAN was aimed at building a strategic alliance as a balance against China.

"This visit was about enhancing Japan's ties with ASEAN," he said. "We believe that this will be conducive to creating peace and stability in the entire Asia-Pacific region, and it will benefit everybody in the region."
Hashimoto ended his trip to Vietnam with a visit to a Japanese school, where he shook hands with children and chucked them affectionately under the chin.
